chunks: Rijal al-Kashshi: Muhammad ibn Mas'ud, from Ali ibn al-Hasan, from his father, from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Ubaydah ibn Zurara; and al-Hasan ibn Jahm ibn Bukayr, from his uncle Abdallah ibn Bukayr, from Ubayd ibn Zurara

He said: I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when Bukayr bin A'yan was mentioned, so he (peace be upon him) said: May Allah have mercy on Bukayr, and He has done it [already], so I looked at him [in surprise], and I was then young in age, so he (peace be upon him) said: I do say 'If Allah wills'.

key_terms.أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu Abdillah, title of Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)
key_terms.إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ: If Allah wills, a phrase denoting divine will
key_terms.بَكِيرُ بْنُ أَعْيَنَ: Bukayr bin A'yan, a companion of the Imams
key_terms.حَدِيثَ السِّنِّ: Young in age, referring to youth or inexperience

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of Imam al-Sadiq's statement 'May Allah have mercy on Bukayr, and He has done it'?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Kashi highlights the Imam’s precise use of 'Insha'Allah' to affirm divine decree while avoiding the implication of compulsion (jabr), a key nuance in Shia theological discourse on free will. The incident underscores the importance of linguistic precision in expressing tawhid, as the young Ubayd ibn Zurara initially misinterpreted the brevity of the Imam’s statement. It serves as a practical lesson in how the Imams balanced affirming God’s will with human agency.
